text:
Envelope framing laws done, which closes the last item on this bead.

FrameCodecLawSuite (8 tests). The governing law is chunk independence: the frames
recovered from a stream must not depend on how the stream was cut up. Existing
FrameCodecSuite only split a single frame at a single point; these generate many
frames and arbitrary chunkings, and state the claim twice -- once as equality
with the original payloads, once as agreement between two different chunkings of
the same stream, which makes a chunk-sensitive bug show up as the decoder
disagreeing with itself.

Also verified a claim FrameDecoder.readLength documents but nothing tested: a
header with its top bit set arrives as a negative int and must be refused as an
invalid length rather than believed. Plus prefix behaviour (a truncated stream
yields a prefix of the frames and finish agrees with boundary alignment),
encode's empty/at-limit/past-limit boundaries, and oversize headers refused
before the claimed payload is buffered.

AgentMessageCodecLawSuite (11 tests). Laws stated over the composed transport --
encode, frame, arbitrary chunking, reassemble, decode -- because testing the JSON
alone leaves the seam with the framing untested. Covers single messages,
pipelined messages in order, wrong schema refused by name, unsupported major
refused as a version failure rather than as malformed JSON, never-throws on
arbitrary BYTES including invalid UTF-8 (a frame payload is whatever the peer
put in it), canonical determinism, and that construction refuses exactly the
reserved extension names, no wider and no narrower.

The distinctive one: this codec's forward compatibility is not tolerance but
preservation -- an unrecognized field is surfaced as an extension. So the law
asserts the field comes back in extensions, since a decoder that dropped it
would satisfy "does not reject" while discarding what a newer peer sent.

Both suites carry sensitivity guards rather than only non-vacuity ones. The
framing one builds the naive reader the law exists to rule out -- one frame per
chunk, which is what you write if you only ever test whole frames -- and asserts
the law disagrees with it while agreeing with the real decoder.

499 tests pass, up from 480. Formatting clean.
